after: ## Claim, fact, topic, preference: four things that are not the same
alt: A decision tree. A statement that asserts nothing is a topic (“Homework.”). One that reports a personal taste is a preference. One that no reasonable person would dispute is a fact (“The school day currently ends at 3.30 p.m.”). Only a statement a reasonable person could dispute is a claim, which needs a defence.
caption: Ask: could a reasonable person disagree, and would I need evidence to persuade them?

alt: Five rows name kinds of claim with the lesson’s examples: fact or existence (bypass noise), definition (a library is public infrastructure), cause (later start times improve test scores), value (charging children is wrong) and policy (restore the library’s hours). Cause needs a causal link; policy needs a problem and a workable remedy.
caption: Knowing the kind of claim tells you what the defence must show.

after: ## Making a claim defensible and interesting
alt: Four tests for a strong claim, arguable, specific, supportable and significant, sit above three upgrades: an obvious statement about social media, a vague one about school lunches and a statement about opinions on uniforms each become a specific position a reader could dispute.
caption: A strong claim takes a side, names specifics and invites the question “Why?”

alt: A tree with the main claim at the top branching to three sub-claims, usually one per paragraph. Below, the main claim may be explicit and quotable, implicit and deduced from evidence and tone, or built toward and revealed at the end.
caption: Find the main claim however it is presented, then list the sub-claims that support it.

after: ## Worked example 2: turning an obvious statement into a claim
alt: A ladder of revisions: “Technology is changing how we learn” gains a specific technology (tablets), a specific setting (school classrooms) and a two-sided assertion, producing “Tablets in school classrooms improve pupils’ access to information but weaken their ability to read at length.”
caption: Each change adds specificity, scope or a disputable position.

after: ## Reading tip: ask the sentence the "so what?" question
alt: Two columns. A claim, “Homework in primary schools does more harm than good”, draws replies such as “Why?” and “No, I don’t think so.” A fact, “The school day currently ends at 3.30 p.m.”, draws “Is that so?” and “OK.”
caption: A claim invites “Why?”; a fact invites “OK.”
